doc.title: Hal Galper interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 27, 2022

title: How jazz has changed: education focuses on note choice
summary: Asked how jazz has changed since the 1960s-70s, Galper blames a lack of understanding of rhythm and jazz education that sells information.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Well you mentioned something in passing, that one of the last generations that enjoyed or employed the apprenticeship —

System in jazz. And this is a broad question but when you reflect back on let’s say the mid-60s into the mid-70s, if you can think back of how you felt about jazz, what you observed about jazz, and if you look at jazz now, let’s say in this century, do you think there are major differences for you?
For me? What do you mean for me?

You were involved in this music when the club scene was different, the recording scene was different, and now things have their own way of being in the jazz world. I guess I’m asking what do you think has changed significantly and that it affects the music the most?
Lack of understanding of the rhythm. Because everything is focused on note choice.
Is that because of jazz education?
Yeah. They can sell that. You can’t sell the rhythm. But they can sell information.
Well said. That’s a good point. You can’t justify a four year jazz program by just or focusing on the rhythm I don’t think. The pedagogy won’t sustain.
